title: Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance
directAnswer: There are O(n²) pair distances and we want the k-th smallest WITHOUT materialising them. Sort the array, then binary search on the *distance value* d in [0, max − min]: for each candidate d, count how many pairs have distance ≤ d using a two-pointer sweep in O(n). Because that count is monotonic in d, the smallest d whose count is ≥ k is exactly the k-th smallest distance. Total O(n log n + n log W) where W is the value range.

remember.pattern: Binary search on the answer + two-pointer feasibility count
remember.formula:
sort(nums)
lo, hi = 0, nums[-1] - nums[0]
while lo < hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if countPairs(mid) >= k:   # enough pairs within distance mid
        hi = mid
    else:
        lo = mid + 1
return lo

countPairs(d): left = 0; for right: while nums[right]-nums[left] > d: left++; cnt += right-left
rules: **Binary search on the value, not the index.** The search space is the distance range `[0, max − min]`, not array positions.
**Sort first** — the two-pointer count and the 'distance = nums[right] − nums[left]' shortcut both require sorted order.
`countPairs(d)` is **monotonic non-decreasing** in `d`; that monotonicity is the whole reason binary search applies.
Find the **smallest** `d` with `countPairs(d) >= k` → use the `hi = mid` / `lo = mid + 1` lower-bound template and return `lo`.
The two-pointer counter is **O(n)**: `left` only ever moves forward across the whole scan, so it's amortised linear, not nested.
whenToUse: 'k-th smallest/largest value' over an implicit set too big to enumerate (pairs, sums, products)
You can cheaply *count how many candidates are ≤ X* for any X (a monotone feasibility test)
The answer is a number in a known range, and counting is faster than sorting all candidates
'Minimize the maximum' / 'maximize the minimum' / 'k-th by value' phrasings
antiSignals: k is tiny and n is small → just generate and sort all O(n²) distances, far simpler
You need the actual pair, not the distance value → binary-search-on-answer only gives the value
No monotone counting function exists → binary search on the answer doesn't apply
remember.takeaway: This is the flagship 'binary search on the answer' problem: when you can't afford to list all candidates but you *can* count how many are ≤ X, binary search the value. Pair it with a two-pointer count and an O(n²) problem collapses to O(n log n + n log W). The same recipe solves Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix, Split Array Largest Sum, and Koko Eating Bananas.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise that 'k-th smallest pair distance' is a binary-search-on-the-answer problem rather than a sort-everything problem, and whether you can build the O(n) monotone counting function with two pointers and prove it's amortised linear.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Generating all O(n²) distances (TLE / MLE at n = 10⁴), or writing the pair counter with a nested loop (O(n²) per binary-search step), or forgetting to sort before counting.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the technique ('binary search on the answer'), justify monotonicity of `countPairs`, and explain why the two-pointer counter is O(n) because `left` never resets. Then connect it to Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix and Split Array Largest Sum.

problemStatement:
The **distance** of a pair of integers `a` and `b` is defined as the absolute difference between `a` and `b`.

Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **k-th smallest distance among all the pairs** `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` where `0 <= i < j < nums.length`.
constraints: k is 1-indexed (k = 1 is the smallest distance)
understanding: Among the n·(n−1)/2 unordered pairs, every pair has a non-negative distance. We want the k-th smallest of those distances by value (duplicates count separately). With n up to 10⁴ there are up to ~5·10⁷ pairs — listing them is borderline, so the intended solution never builds the list: it binary searches the distance value and counts pairs within a candidate distance in linear time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k 1-indexed or 0-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1-indexed. k = 1 asks for the smallest distance overall. So I'm looking for the smallest distance value d such that at least k pairs have distance ≤ d.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array have duplicate values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Duplicates create distance-0 pairs, and each pair is counted independently. My counting function handles that naturally since it counts pairs, not distinct values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n, and can I just enumerate all pair distances?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: n can be 10⁴, so there are up to ~5·10⁷ pairs. Building and sorting them is O(n² log n) and ~50M ints of memory — risky for time and space. I'll binary search the answer instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need the actual pair or just the distance?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the distance value, which is exactly what binary-search-on-the-answer returns. If they wanted the pair, I'd reconstruct it afterward.

examples.explanation: Pairs and distances: (1,3)→2, (1,1)→0, (3,1)→2. Sorted distances: [0, 2, 2]. The 1st smallest is 0.
All three pairs have distance 0, so the 2nd smallest distance is still 0.
Sorted [1, 1, 6]. Distances: (1,1)→0, (1,6)→5, (1,6)→5 → sorted [0, 5, 5]. The 3rd smallest is 5.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Too many pairs to enumerate, but pairs ≤ d are easy to count → binary search the distance value.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Enumerate and Sort All Distances
approaches.whenToMention: State it first to establish correctness and the O(n²) cost, then explain why it won't scale to n = 10⁴ and pivot to binary search on the answer.
hints: The most literal reading: every pair has a distance. How many pairs are there, and what would you do with all their distances?
Compute the absolute difference for every pair (i, j) with i < j and collect them into a list.
Sort the list and return the element at index k − 1 (k is 1-indexed).
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n(n−1)/2 ≈ n²/2 pairs to generate, and sorting that many distances costs O(n² log n). The list itself holds O(n²) integers.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate all `n(n−1)/2` pairs with two nested loops, push each absolute difference into a list, sort the list, and return the `(k−1)`-th entry.

**Why it's obviously correct.** It materialises the exact multiset the problem talks about — every pairwise distance — and then 'k-th smallest' is just an array index after sorting. There's no cleverness to get wrong; it's the definition turned into code, which makes it the perfect baseline to state before optimising.

**Why it doesn't scale.** With `n = 10⁴`, the pair count is about `5 × 10⁷`. Generating them is ~50 million operations (tolerable), but *storing* 50 million integers is ~200 MB and *sorting* them is `O(n² log n)` ≈ `5 × 10⁷ × 26` ≈ `1.3 × 10⁹` comparisons — both blow the typical time and memory limits. The bottleneck is that we pay to produce *every* distance even though we only want *one* of them.

**The key realisation that leads to the better solution.** We don't need the sorted list — we only need to know *which value* sits at rank `k`. If, for any candidate distance `d`, we could quickly answer 'how many pairs have distance ≤ `d`?', we could binary search for the smallest `d` whose count reaches `k`. That count turns out to be computable in `O(n)` after sorting, which is what the optimal approach exploits.
approaches.insight: Sorting all distances answers far more than the question asks — it ranks every pair when we only want rank k. Whenever you catch yourself fully sorting an implicit set to grab one element, ask whether you can instead *count items ≤ X* and binary search X. Counting is almost always cheaper than ranking everything.

dryRun.intro: Generate every pair's distance, sort, then index k − 1 = 0.

java.explanation: Pre-size for every unordered pair — this is the O(n²) memory that sinks the approach at scale.
Absolute difference is the pair distance; j > i avoids counting a pair twice.
k is 1-indexed, so the k-th smallest sits at index k − 1 after sorting.

python.explanation: j starts at i + 1 so each unordered pair is generated exactly once.
Collect the distance of every pair into one big list.
k-th smallest = index k − 1 after sorting.

pitfalls: Allocating ~n²/2 integers — out of memory for n near 10⁴.
Indexing with `dists[k]` instead of `dists[k - 1]` — off by one because k is 1-indexed.
Submitting this as the final answer on the hard variant — it TLEs/MLEs at the upper constraints.

approaches.name: Binary Search on the Answer + Two-Pointer Count (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended solution. Lead with 'binary search the distance value, not the index', then describe the O(n) counting sweep and its monotonicity.

complexity.time: O(n log n + n log W)

hints: You don't need every distance — only the value at rank k. Suppose you could ask 'how many pairs have distance ≤ d?' cheaply. How would that pin down the answer?
Sort the array. Then `countPairs(d)` is monotonic: bigger d never decreases the count. Binary search the smallest d with `countPairs(d) >= k`.

Compute `countPairs(d)` with two pointers on the sorted array: for each `right`, advance `left` while `nums[right] − nums[left] > d`; then every index in `[left, right)` pairs with `right`, so add `right − left`. The `left` pointer never moves backward → O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). The binary search runs O(log W) iterations where W = max − min ≤ 10⁶, and each iteration does an O(n) two-pointer count → O(n log W). Only a handful of scalars are used → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort `nums`. The smallest possible distance is `0` and the largest is `nums[n-1] − nums[0]`, so the answer lives in `[0, nums[n-1] − nums[0]]`. Binary search that *value* range for the smallest distance `d` such that at least `k` pairs have distance `≤ d`.

**Why binary search on the value works — monotonicity.** Define `countPairs(d)` = number of pairs with distance `≤ d`. As `d` grows, no pair ever leaves the 'within distance' set and some may join, so `countPairs` is non-decreasing in `d`. That makes the predicate `countPairs(d) >= k` a monotone step function: false for small `d`, then true forever after some threshold. Binary search locates that threshold — and the threshold value is precisely the k-th smallest distance, because just below it fewer than `k` pairs qualify and exactly at it the count first reaches `k`.

**Why the count uses two pointers and is O(n).** On the *sorted* array, for a fixed right endpoint `right`, the pairs ending at `right` with distance `≤ d` are exactly those whose left value is `≥ nums[right] − d`. Because the array is sorted, those left endpoints form a contiguous block `[left, right)`. We maintain `left` as the smallest index with `nums[right] − nums[left] <= d`. As `right` advances, the required `left` can only move *forward* (a larger `nums[right]` needs an equal-or-larger lower bound), so across the entire scan `left` travels at most `n` steps total. Each `right` contributes `right − left` pairs. One forward sweep of two pointers — `O(n)`, not `O(n²)`.

**Why the lower-bound template (`hi = mid`, return `lo`).** We want the *smallest* `d` satisfying the predicate, so this is a left-boundary search. When `countPairs(mid) >= k`, `mid` is a feasible distance but maybe not the smallest, so keep it: `hi = mid`. When `countPairs(mid) < k`, `mid` is too small, so `lo = mid + 1`. With `while (lo < hi)` the window converges to the threshold and we return `lo`. Note we binary search on a *value*, so there's no array index to read at `mid` — `mid` is itself a candidate distance.

**Why sorting is mandatory.** Two facts depend on it: (1) the max distance is `last − first`, giving tight search bounds; (2) the two-pointer count relies on left endpoints forming a contiguous sorted block. Without sorting, counting pairs `≤ d` would itself be `O(n²)` and the whole speed-up evaporates. Sorting costs `O(n log n)` once, dwarfed by neither term.

**Putting the complexity together.** Sort `O(n log n)`; then `O(log W)` binary-search steps (`W ≤ 10⁶`, so ~20 steps) each doing an `O(n)` count → `O(n log W)`. No `O(n²)` list, `O(1)` auxiliary space. This comfortably handles `n = 10⁴`.
approaches.insight: The pivot from O(n²) to near-linear is the realisation that *counting how many candidates are ≤ X* is exponentially cheaper than *sorting all candidates*. Binary search on the answer turns 'find the k-th value' into 'find the threshold where the count crosses k'. The two-pointer counter is the workhorse that makes each threshold test O(n). This count-then-binary-search shape recurs in Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix, Split Array Largest Sum, and Koko Eating Bananas.

java.explanation: Sorting enables both the tight [0, last − first] bounds and the contiguous two-pointer count.
Search the DISTANCE VALUE range, not array indices — min distance 0, max distance last − first.
Monotone predicate: enough pairs within distance mid → mid is feasible, look for something smaller.
Lower-bound template: keep mid as a candidate, never mid − 1.
Too few pairs within mid → the answer distance must be larger.
Shrink the window from the left until nums[right] − nums[left] ≤ dist.
Every index in [left, right) pairs with right inside distance dist → add that many pairs.

python.explanation: Mandatory: the count and the bounds both assume sorted order.
Advance left until the pair (left, right) is within dist; left never moves backward → O(n) total.
right − left pairs end at `right` with distance ≤ dist.
Distance value search space: 0 up to the spread of the array.
Feasible — shrink the upper bound (hi = mid) to hunt for the smallest such distance.
Smallest distance whose pair-count reaches k = the k-th smallest distance.

diagrams.title: How countPairs(d) sweeps with two pointers
diagrams.caption: For each right endpoint, left advances until the pair fits within d; right − left pairs are added. left never resets.

edgeCases.behavior: max distance is 0 → lo = hi = 0 from the start, loop body never runs, return 0.
Sorted [1, 1, 6]; binary searches [0, 5]. countPairs reaches 3 only at d = 5 → returns 5.
Asks for the maximum distance; the predicate is only satisfied at d = last − first, so lo converges to hi.

edgeCases.input: All elements distinct and far apart
edgeCases.behavior: countPairs(0) = 0 forces lo upward; the search still terminates in O(log W) steps.

pitfalls: Binary searching over array indices instead of the distance value range.
Forgetting to sort — the two-pointer count becomes wrong and O(n²).
Writing countPairs with a nested loop (resetting left each right) — that's O(n²) per step, killing the speed-up.
Using `hi = mid - 1` for this lower-bound search — can skip the exact threshold distance.
Counting ordered pairs (doubling) — use `right − left`, which counts each unordered pair once.

commonMistakes: Enumerating all O(n²) pair distances and sorting — TLE/MLE at n = 10⁴.
Binary searching the index range instead of the distance value range.
Implementing the pair counter with a nested loop, making each binary-search step O(n²).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Resetting the left pointer each iteration (nested O(n²) count)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If `left` restarts at 0 for every `right`, the counter is O(n²) per binary-search step → O(n² log W) overall, no better than brute force. The whole point is that `left` only moves forward across the entire sweep.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Binary searching indices instead of the distance value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The k-th smallest distance is a *value* in [0, max − min], not an index into the array. Searching index bounds is a category error — there's no sorted-by-distance array to index into.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to sort before counting
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The two-pointer count assumes that left endpoints within distance d form a contiguous block, which only holds on sorted data. Skipping the sort makes the count silently wrong.

patternNote: The canonical 'binary search on the answer' with a monotone counting predicate. Recognise it whenever you need the k-th value of an implicit set too large to enumerate but where 'how many are ≤ X' is cheap to compute. Pairing it with a two-pointer count gives the linear feasibility test; the same recipe powers Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix, Split Array Largest Sum, and Koko Eating Bananas.
